column4: Description
An open iron helmet with a wide brim, cheap and good against blows and arrows from above. The common soldier's helmet.
The helmet of the Wars of the Roses: a smooth steel skull with a long tail over the neck and a visor that lifts.
A sallet worn with a bevor, a steel plate that guards the chin and throat. Little is left open but the eyes.
A close helmet from Italy that shuts around the whole head with hinged cheek plates. A knight's helmet, costly and stifling.
A plaited straw hat for the harvest field. It keeps the sun and a little rain off, and nothing else.
A brown wool-felt hat, the everyday headwear of townsmen and yeomen.
A close white linen cap tied under the chin. Almost everyone wears one, alone or under a hat.
A padded cap worn under a helmet to soften blows and stop the steel from chafing.
A hood with a short cape over the shoulders, the usual wear for the road in wind and rain.
A parti-coloured hood with ass's ears and bells, worn by jesters and at feast-day revels.
A farm billhook on a long shaft, with a spike and a hook added for war. It cuts, stabs and drags riders from the saddle: the English foot soldier's weapon.
Axe blade, hammer and spike on one shaft, made to break plate armour. The weapon of knights fighting on foot.
A long straight sword with a grip for two hands, quick in the cut and fine in the thrust. A gentleman's weapon.
The straight one-handed sword worn at the hip by men-at-arms, often used with a buckler.
A broad single-edged sword that cuts like a cleaver. Cheaper than a knightly sword and brutal against unarmoured men.
A small hammer head backed by a spike, made to dent and pierce plate where a sword edge would only skate.
A flanged steel head on a short haft. It needs no edge and cares little for mail.
An ash shaft with a leaf-shaped iron head: the oldest and cheapest weapon of war, and still one of the best.
A man-tall bow of yew. It takes years to learn, and English law makes every man practise at the butts on Sundays.
A steel or horn bow on a stock, spanned with a lever or windlass. Slow to load, easy to aim, and it hits hard.
A stout wooden club. Every village has a few, and the law can hardly forbid a stick.
A straight ash staff taller than a man: a walking stick on the road and a fast, far-reaching weapon in trained hands.
A felling axe from the woodpile. A tool first, but it splits a shield as well as a log.
A small round steel shield held in the fist, used with a sword to turn blows and punch. Worn hung on the belt in town.
A candle lantern with windows of thin scraped horn: light for the road that the wind can't blow out.
A tall wooden shield that a crossbowman props up and shelters behind while he loads, painted with the badge of York.
A tall wooden shield that a crossbowman props up and shelters behind while he loads, painted with the badge of Lancaster.
A flat-topped wooden shield faced with painted leather. Old-fashioned by 1455, but it still stops a blade.
A flat-topped wooden shield faced with painted leather. Old-fashioned by 1455, but it still stops a blade.
A heavy cloak of undyed wool, greasy enough to shed rain. Bed and blanket to anyone sleeping rough.
A travelling cloak with its own hood, for long days on the road in English weather.
Fine dyed wool lined with fur. The law says who may wear which furs, so it shows rank as well as keeping out the cold.
A stiff spike of a dagger with a round guard and pommel, made to be driven through the gaps in armour.
The common man's dagger, named for the two round lobes of its guard. Worn at the front of the belt by nearly everyone.
A plain single-edged knife for eating and work. Everyone carries one; few think of it as a weapon.
A linen bag with a leather spacer that holds a sheaf of 24 arrows and keeps their feathers dry.
A leather purse hung from the belt. Cutpurses are named for what they do to the thongs.
A stave wrapped in tallow-soaked rags. Bright, smoky, and gone within the hour.
Many layers of linen quilted into a thick coat. Worn alone it is the poor soldier's armour; it turns cuts and smothers blows.
A fitted padded doublet with laces to tie plate armour onto. Lighter than a jack, and made to be worn under steel.
A knee-length tunic of undyed wool: what most of England wears most days.
A jacket in the red of the Nevilles with their white saltire. Wearing a lord's livery says whose man you are.
A short open-sided coat worn over armour, showing a coat of arms so that friend can tell friend in the press.
A long pleated gown of fine dyed cloth with hanging sleeves, belted at the waist. Not for working in, which is the point.
A haubergeon: thousands of riveted iron rings reaching to the thigh. Proof against cuts, less so against points and hammers.
A skirt of mail hung from the waist to guard the hips and groin where plate leaves gaps.
Small steel plates riveted inside a cloth jacket, the rivet heads showing in rows. Flexible, strong, and favoured by archers and captains alike.
Iron plates sewn between layers of canvas. The cheap cousin of the brigandine, made in every market town.
A complete suit of plate: breast and back, arms and legs, made to measure. A fortune in steel, and it lets a trained man run, ride and fight.
A collar of linked S-shapes, the badge of the House of Lancaster. The king gives it to those who serve him.
A collar of suns and white roses, the badges of the House of York, given to its trusted men.
Plain leather gloves for riding, hawking and hard work.
Steel mitten gauntlets over leather gloves. A sword hand without them is soon a hand without fingers.
Side-laced turnshoes of soft leather with a flat sole and no heel. They wear through in a season.
Tall soft boots that reach the thigh and fold down for walking. They keep the legs from the saddle and the mud.
Jointed steel shoes that cover the foot, the last piece of a full harness.
